Meeting header:
2026-03-16 15:00 UTC | Duration: ~58m | Redwood: Liam/Priya/Miguel/Jules | Customer: Sasha/Daniel/Anita/Tom/Grace

Summary (auto-generated, may be incomplete):
Deep dive on Redwood Private (VPC) security architecture. Focus on network isolation, ingress/egress controls, firewalling, and compliance artifacts (SOC2/ISO, audit logs, KMS). Customer raised concerns about control plane connectivity, key management, and egress inspection. Agreed next steps: share diagrams, pilot checklist, and schedule benchmarking.

Topics: network isolation, control plane vs data plane, ingress patterns, egress whitelisting, VPC endpoints, NAT/bastion, WAF/NGFW, IDS/IDS, VPC Flow Logs, audit log retention, KMS/HSM integration, SSO/RBAC, certs and rotation.

Transcript:
[00:00] Liam Carter: All right sorry, thanks everyone for joining. We're here to walk through the end-to-end Private VPC architecture and specifically the security controls — Sasha, Anita, you mentioned you wanted to cover network isolation and auditability, correct?
[00:12] Sasha Kim: Yes, thanks Liam. Main asks: 1) no customer data leaves our VPC unencrypted, 2) clear audit trail for all admin actions, 3) control plane separation — we need to understand what touches the internet and how.
[00:22] Priya Nand: Totally. We'll go through the control plane vs data plane split, and then dive into ingress/egress patterns. I'll also highlight where we integrate with your KMS and audit systems.
[00:30] Daniel Rivera: Quick note — our compliance team will require SOC 2 artifacts and proof of key rotation, and we need to validate the network flows before we allow any production traffic.
[00:39] Miguel Santos: Yep and we can provide our SOC 2 attestation and ISO certs, but we'll also map the log paths to your SIEM — Splunk/Elastic, whatever you use — we stream audit logs over a customer-controlled collector.
[00:50] [00:50] Anita Patel: Can you clarify the control plane placement? Is the Redwood control plane hosted in Redwood's cloud, and the data plane entirely in our VPC? How do you handle orchestration updates — do they require outbound internet?
[01:02] Priya Nand: Good question. For Private deployments we offer two patterns: 1) Managed private where customer network peered with Redwood control plane over a secured mTLS channel, and 2) Fully customer-hosted on-prem where both control and data plane are in your environment. In the managed private model, the data plane (inference pods, KV caches, model storage) run in your VPC/subnets; control plane calls are outbound-only from a small set of egress IPs and they use mutual TLS and client certs.
[01:28] Tom Wallace: So that implies some allowed egress to Redwood's control endpoint, right — can you give an IP range or FQDN we can allowlist?
[01:36] Liam Carter: Yes, we'll share a /26-range and FQDNs. For HA we use multiple regions — we'll provide region-specific lists. We also support using a private link / transit gateway so control plane traffic never goes out to the public internet if you'd prefer.
[01:50] Sasha Kim: PrivateLink is preferred for us. We need zero direct internet egress for the inference nodes, unless it's to an approved endpoint.
[01:58] Priya Nand: Absolutely. For PrivateLink / VPC endpoint model, all S3/model fetch and control plane traffic can go over VPC endpoints. For example, model artifacts can be pulled from an S3 bucket via an S3 VPC endpoint, and management traffic via PrivateLink. No NAT required.
[02:12] [02:12] Miguel Santos: Quick note — some of the pre-built accelerators we use reach out for kernel updates in certain deployments; in Private deployments that is configurable and can be disabled or proxied through your patching infrastructure.
[02:24] Sasha Kim: We will insist on disabling any outbound update checks unless they're routed through our update proxies.
[02:30] Priya Nand: Noted.
[02:33] [02:33] Anita Patel: On firewalling — do you recommend SGs only, or a layered NGFW? We have Palo Alto Prisma in our stack.
[02:40] Miguel Santos: Layered approach: security groups for instance-level L3/L4 control, NACLs for subnet-level additional guardrails, and NGFW for L7 inspection and threat detection. For high-throughput inference egress, we usually place an NGFW at the egress subnets and use route tables to direct traffic.
[02:57] Daniel Rivera: How does that interact with autoscaling? We scale pods rapidly, tens per minute — we don't want to perforate the firewall.
[03:05] Priya Nand: We recommend placing the NGFW in a centralized egress VPC with an autoscaling set of egress NATs/bastions + a load balancer. The data plane nodes talk to the egress via a well-known route, and the firewall scales horizontally. That keeps per-node CPU low.
[03:18] [03:18] Tom Wallace: Regarding egress, we need strict whitelisting to only allow calls to (1) Redwood control plane PrivateLink endpoints, (2) S3 endpoint for model artifacts, (3) our internal telemetry collectors, and (4) updates proxy. Can you support explicit allowlists?
[03:32] Priya Nand: Yes we can. We have an allowlist template. Also we support DNS-based allowlisting for FQDNs, but strongly recommend IP-based allowlist to avoid DNS spoofing.
[03:43] Sasha Kim: Audit logs — what's captured? We need admin action logs, API calls, model deployments, config changes, and both control-plane and data-plane events. Retention needs are 3 years for some artifacts.
[03:55] Miguel Santos: We capture admin API events, model versioning events, CA logs for cert issuance, and operational events from the nodes. Logs can be forwarded to your SIEM with a guaranteed TLS stream. For long-term retention we can deliver compressed archives to your S3 with server-side encryption (SSE-KMS) and lifecycle policies.
[04:14] Anita Patel: Do you maintain immutable audit logs or do you support WORM?
[04:18] Priya Nand: We can write immutable archives via S3 Object Lock if you want WORM-style retention. We also support pushing signed audit bundles to a customer-controlled bucket.
[04:27] [04:27] Daniel Rivera: KMS integration — do you use our KMS or Redwood's? We require keys to be customer-managed and stored in our HSM-backed KMS.
[04:36] Liam Carter: For Private we support customer-managed keys (CMK) in AWS KMS or customer HSM. Data at rest is encrypted with envelope encryption — service generates data key which is encrypted with your CMK. You keep key rotation and access control. Redwood never has plaintext keys.
[04:50] Miguel Santos: Also note: for models we support per-tenant key wrapping so each tenant's artifacts are encrypted with separate keys.
[04:58] Sasha Kim: How about secrets for service accounts inside the cluster? We're concerned about leakage in case of node compromise.
[05:05] Priya Nand: Secrets are injected at runtime from your KMS-backed secrets store — we recommend using a secrets manager with IAM roles for service accounts. The pods do not persist secrets to disk; they live in memory and the runtime zeroes them after use.
[05:18] [05:18] Anita Patel: For network monitoring, can we get VPC Flow Logs, and do you collect packet captures for debugging?
[05:25] Miguel Santos: We can enable VPC Flow Logs to your Log Archive. Packet capture is sensitive; for debugging we do ephemeral captures that are stored in your S3 and optionally pushed to your forensic team. All captures are encrypted and access audited.
[05:40] Tom Wallace: What about mTLS between components? Do pods use mTLS?
[05:45] Priya Nand: Yes. Internal RPCs use mutual TLS with short-lived certs issued by an internal CA. For customer-hosted control plane we can integrate with your PKI to issue certs.
[05:56] [05:56] Sasha Kim: Regarding RBAC/SSO: we want integration with Okta and SCIM provisioning, and fine-grained RBAC so developers don't have access to production inference logs.
[06:05] Miguel Santos: We support SAML/Okta SSO and SCIM user sync. RBAC is role-based and you can create system roles and custom roles — with audit logs for all privilege escalations.
[06:16] Daniel Rivera: Any additional compliance artifacts? Pen test reports, network diagrams for auditors?
[06:22] Liam Carter: We'll provide SOC 2 Type II report, ISO 27001 cert, and a pen-test summary. For detailed architecture we can provide network diagrams, segmentation maps, and routing tables for the pilot environment.
[06:33] [06:33] Anita Patel: We also need to understand how model caching is handled — KV cache typically stores prefixes; is that encrypted?
[06:41] Priya Nand: KV caches are encrypted at rest and we can store them on encrypted EBS volumes or in-memory only, depending on your preference. For strict non-persistence we can run them ephemeral-only in RAM.
[06:54] [06:54] Tom Wallace: Performance impact — if we force PrivateLink + NGFW + deep inspection, what's the latency hit? We need 95th < 200ms for short prompts.
[07:05] Miguel Santos: There is some overhead. In our internal benchmarks, PrivateLink adds minimal overhead (sub-5ms), but NGFW L7 inspection can add 15–40ms depending on throughput and rules. For strict SLOs we recommend bypassing deep L7 for low-latency inference paths and applying L7 inspection on admin/management traffic and async telemetry.
[07:26] Liam Carter: That's a common compromise — data path optimized for latency, control/telemetry path for inspection. We can run a short pilot to measure the delta with your expected payload sizes.
[07:36] [07:36] Grace Huang: Legal question — is there a data residency guarantee? Some of our EU customers' data must remain in EU.
[07:43] Priya Nand: Yes. You can pin resources to region. For Private we deploy everything in your chosen region. We can confirm model artifact geo-location and backup policies.
[07:53] [07:53] Sasha Kim: On incident response — we want playbooks and an escalation matrix that ties to our on-call.
[07:59] Jules Meyer: We'll include an incident response annex — contact numbers, SLAs, and roles. For pilot we'll have a runbook and joint run of our incident simulation.
[08:10] [08:10] Anita Patel: A small nit — DNS leaks: how do you prevent nodes from using public DNS?
[08:15] Priya Nand: We configure VPC DNS to use your resolver and disallow 53/udp to the internet, and enforce DNS over TLS where available.
[08:24] [08:24] Daniel Rivera: For egress logging we want per-flow logs with user-ids where possible, and correlation ID support upstream so we can trace a request end-to-end.
[08:33] Miguel Santos: We can propagate X-Request-ID headers and annotate logs with tenant and request IDs. Flow logs will include ENI and port-level details — you can map to request IDs in the app logs.
[08:44] [08:44] Sasha Kim: Anything else we should be aware of?
[08:47] Priya Nand: Just one more: cert rotation. We support short-lived certs via your PKI or our internal CA, and automated rotation workflows with no downtime.
[08:58] Tom Wallace: Ok that helps. Next steps as we discussed: send diagrams, allowlist, pilot checklist. We'll gather the network profile and share.
[09:07] Liam Carter: Great. We'll follow up with all the docs and the SOC2/ISO pack. Thanks everyone.
